initial_observation.chief_complaint: accidental chest injury from an air rifle
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The entry wound, measuring 5 mm, was located on the lower sternum, with no exit wound. The patient experienced chest pain but did not have difficulty breathing or abdominal pain at the time of admission. Upon admission, the patient displayed stable vital signs, with normal breathing rates, equal air entry on both sides, and maintained oxygen saturation on air. The abdomen was soft, and the patient had a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 15/15, indicating no focal neurological deficits.

evidence_items.source_text: four hours after admission, the child suffered two episodes of generalized tonic-clonic convulsions, each lasting less than two minutes, accompanied by a reduction in consciousness level. Subsequent neurological examination revealed weakness in the left upper and lower limbs, along with contralateral facial weakness.

Initial evaluations, including plain chest X-ray and extended FAST scan, did not reveal the presence of a lodged pellet in the chest or any signs of pneumo- or hemothorax. However, a minimal pericardial effusion was observed in the extended FAST scan.
The 2D Echocardiography showed a thin layer of pericardial effusion.

After the development of neurological symptoms and signs, we did the non-contrast CT scan of the brain (NCCT brain) revealed a hyperdense pellet near the right base of the skull, adjacent to the carotid canal. Additionally, hyperdensity observed in the middle cerebral artery indicated a thrombus in the right middle cerebral artery.
evidence_items.temporal_cue: after the development of neurological symptoms

evidence_items.source_text: A contrast-enhanced CT scan (CECT) of the head, neck, and thorax confirmed the presence of the pellet embolism in the right internal carotid artery, located within the carotid foramen at the inferior opening of the carotid canal. This imaging also indicated non-opacification of the right internal carotid artery and proximal carotid artery, suggesting a thrombus causing an acute cerebral infarction in the right cerebral territory. The CECT scan further showed minimal pericardial and pleural effusion.
A Carotid duplex study provided valuable insights, revealing turbid flow within the right internal carotid artery, linked to distal obstruction by the pellet. However, no dissection flaps were noted.
Due to the acute cerebral edema resulting from the cerebral infarction, a decompressive craniotomy was performed to alleviate the mass effect.

Subsequently, a thorough evaluation utilizing a four-vessel cerebral Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) was conducted to assess the cerebral vasculature and attempt the retrieval of foreign bodies. During the procedure, efforts were made to aspirate the thrombus in the proximal internal carotid artery (ICA) using the penumbral clot retrieval system (Fig.

Despite successful advancement of guide wires into the distal ICA, bypassing the foreign body, attempts to advance various snare-type devices and balloon catheters past the tightly wedged foreign body were unsuccessful. The foreign body was firmly lodged within the ICA, impeding further advancement of these instruments. Efforts were made to dislodge the pellet by applying a maximum suction of 100 kPa via the penumbra catheter, but regrettably, dislodgment could not be achieved. Additionally, the DSA revealed no cross-circulation from the left ICA, further complicating the situation and limiting potential alternative approaches.

After two weeks of comprehensive and specialized inpatient care, the patient unfortunately sustained permanent hemiplegia, a significant and lasting disability. Given this outcome, the medical team arranged for the patient to be transferred to a dedicated rehabilitation center where they could receive rehabilitation and occupational therapy.
evidence_items.temporal_cue: after two weeks of inpatient care
